newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS - Bonds and bears hurt Danish banks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bonds and bears hurt Danish banks.

text.p: A depressed bond market and gloomy predictions by British investment bank James Capel rocked top Danish bank shares on Wednesday, despite their fat securities earnings and general popularity with investors.
Capel downgraded Den Danske Bank and Unidanmark to 'sell' from 'buy', citing poor 1996 performance that it expected to continue amid increased competition from small and medium-sized banks.
"On our current forecasts and a long-bond yield of 6.8 percent,our valuation work suggests end-1996 fair values of 388 crowns for Den Danske and 271 crowns for Unidanmark," it said.
By the close of trade Unidanmark had plunged seven crowns -- 2.5 percent -- to 273 crowns, after hitting a low of 269.
Den Danske Bank fared slightly better, falling eight crowns to 424 crowns, while BG Bank shed two crowns to 253.

Most Danish shares slumped during the morning, on U.S. market losses and the weakening dollar, but banks took an extra battering after the Capel report and remarks by Bundesbank economist Otmar Issing turned bond prices downward.
Capel echoed other recent misgivings about Danish banks, whose shares have lagged behind those of most other sectors on a generally buoyant Copenhagen bourse.
An analysis by the Berlingske Tidende daily on Monday showed the all-share index had risen 23 percent since the start of 1996 while the banking sector had gone up only 12 percent.

The business daily Borsen last week cited analysts as saying that banks were together expected to earn up to nine billion crowns ($1.54 billion) from 1996 securities trade, after 1995's 10 billion crown bonanza.

But published results show generally disappointing core earnings. Domestic organic growth by the top banks is seen as having peaked and an increasing number of analysts worry about their root strength.
Borsen saw a danger that some banks would forget lacklustre operating profits and expand on the back of their securities earnings.
"This can come back and hit like a boomerang in the coming years when it is considered inconceivable that these (securities) results will repeat themselves," it said.
"The problems that are coming have their origins in the good times," Flemming Rasmussen, vice-president of the banking regulatory authority, told a seminar last week.
He predicted that several banks would disappear by the end of the decade, saying: "More mergers would be healthy. With over 200 financial institutions Denmark is simply over-banked."

James Capel said that the two biggest banks, Den Danske and Unidanmark had already reaped most of the savings possible from earlier mergers, and while there was some growth potential in mortgage banking and insurance, competition would be tough.
"We expect the increased competition to come from the medium and small banks, which are long overdue a bout of consolidation and restructuring," it said.
"Having barely touched their cost bases over the past six years these banks have plenty of scope to improve efficency."
The third-largest bank, BG was formed out of a merger of Bikuben and the post office's Girobank a year ago.
It is seen as a candidate to merge with mortgage heavyweight Nykredit and insurer Topdanmark to create a serious contender to the top two but is keeping its plans to itself.
There is also talk of a marriage between the smaller Amagerbanken and Sydbank.

Until now investors, including many overseas players, have shown few misgivings about the future earnings of the big banks, regarding them as undervalued compared with foreign finance houses and weighting them heavily in their portfolios.
"The movement we saw today may have been a knee-jerk reaction compounded by herd instinct. The market always tends to trade, then think," an economist said.
"I think that it will become clearer over the next six months as more analyses are published and we get the banks' 1996 reports."
--Copenhagen newsroom +45 969650 ($1=5.839 Danish Crown)
